topic: programming languages; mixed-initiative dialog DSLs; human-computer interaction
status: bounded evaluation-design lead from one sampled 2011 full text and one targeted 2025 journal follow-up; no independent reproduction
claim: The sampled 2011 dialog-DSL paper supports formal expressiveness and Scheme proof-of-concept feasibility; its section titled ‘Evaluation’ analyzes the count/structure of representable dialog specifications, not user or task outcomes. A 2025 journal extension adds formal staging semantics, Haskell implementation, and an online-food-order case study with reported expression-compression improvements, so it is incorrect to say the research line remained only a prototype. However, the reviewed descriptions do not establish that DSL compression improves independent authoring time or user task completion, errors, or repair effort. The bounded opportunity is a controlled author/user outcome comparison, not a claim that the DSL lacks practical value.
positive_evidence: The 2011 full text gives a formal characterization/count of dialog specifications and a Scheme proof-of-concept dialog miner/stager; it reports no measured user completion, errors, or authoring time.
The 2025 peer-reviewed journal follow-up formalizes simplification/staging, implements it in Haskell, and models portions of a concurrent online food-ordering dialog.
The 2025 article reports higher representation compression and conceptual comparison to VoiceXML and State Chart XML, evidence beyond the 2011 prototype.
counterevidence: A case study and compression measure are practical evidence; absence of controlled human outcomes does not mean the newer system has no practical utility.
The 2011 paper's formal expressiveness and generated stager are legitimate results even without user evaluation.
Only the two directly related works were checked here; this audit does not establish that no other dialog-authoring user studies exist.

sources.title: The Formal Semantics and Implementation of a Domain-Specific Language for Mixed-Initiative Dialogs
sources.sections: Official journal abstract/results: formal semantics, Haskell implementation, food-order case study, expression compression; conceptual comparison to VoiceXML/SCXML

falsifiable_test: Recruit independent developers to encode the same preregistered mixed-initiative dialog tasks using DSL, VoiceXML, and SCXML, then recruit representative users to execute the resulting systems. Measure authoring time, specification size, defects/repairs, user task completion, time, and recovery errors under matched training and tool budgets. The lead weakens if DSL compression does not replicate across tasks or does not predict author/user benefits; it strengthens if the compression advantage survives independent authoring and improves validated outcomes. This batch ran no user study.
limitations: One 2011 sampled preprint and one targeted 2025 journal follow-up; the 2025 evidence includes a case study but no common controlled user-outcome benchmark was verified. No independent replication, artifact execution, or claim about the entire dialog-systems literature.

topic: programming languages; context-oriented programming; static typing; adaptive systems
status: bounded formal-to-runtime validation lead from one sampled PLACES paper and one targeted COORDINATION full text
claim: The sampled ContextML paper proves progress and subject reduction for well-typed programs under an explicit-context operational semantics, while identifying asynchronous environment evolution and event-driven context changes as future work. A 2012 security extension adds program- and message-triggered context changes, effects, and static model checking, but uses an abstract bus and explicitly leaves a richer coordination model with concurrency, distribution, and asynchrony for future work. The bounded question is whether these model-level guarantees and policies remain predictive in a concrete event-driven runtime—not whether the formal proofs fail within their stated models.
positive_evidence: The sampled six-page paper states ContextML's context explicitly and proves progress plus subject reduction; its typing discipline ensures layered dispatch does not get stuck for well-typed programs.
The 2012 follow-up extends ContextML with resource operations, security policies, message passing, effects, and static policy/protocol model checks.
The follow-up allows context change through program operations and exchanged messages, narrowing the original paper's scope boundary.
counterevidence: The guarantee is mathematically meaningful under the formal semantics; runtime asynchrony is outside that model and does not refute the proof.
The 2012 work models a communication bus and message-triggered context changes, so not all external/environment interaction is absent.
The follow-up explicitly leaves concurrency, distribution, and a stronger asynchronous coordination model for future work; it supplies no deployed runtime cost/violation study.

sources.title: Types for Coordinating Secure Behavioural Variations
sources.sections: Sections 3–6 formal context, effects and policy/protocol checks; Section 7 leaves concurrency/distribution/asynchrony as future work

falsifiable_test: Implement the ContextML semantics and security-policy checks in an event-driven runtime, then generate well-typed programs with delayed, reordered, concurrent, and adversarial context/message events. Compare predicted safety to runtime traces, and measure false positives/negatives, response latency, memory, and analysis overhead. The lead weakens if the published model already covers the tested event semantics and predicts every trace with acceptable overhead; it strengthens if a concrete event pattern violates assumptions or static/runtime costs materially change. No runtime or benchmark was built in this batch.
limitations: Two closely related formal papers from the same research group, not independent validation; no implementation, user system, or empirical runtime measurements. Findings are scoped to their stated operational models.

topic: programming languages; static analysis; control-flow analysis; complexity
status: bounded theory-to-practice comparison lead from one sampled 2009 dissertation and one targeted PLDI 2010 full-text follow-up
claim: The sampled arXiv record is a 2009 Brandeis dissertation (uploaded to arXiv in 2013), not research first conducted in 2013. It proves 0CFA PTIME-complete and fixed-k kCFA EXPTIME-complete for k>0 in its specified higher-order functional formulation; its preface explicitly says it contains no benchmarks or prototype. The PLDI 2010 follow-up resolves the apparent functional-versus-OO conflict by tracing complexity to closure/object representation and derives polynomial m-CFA for functional programs, reporting competitive precision at lower cost on its evaluated cases. Thus worst-case formal complexity must be reported with the language and representation, and does not by itself predict the runtime of every practical program. A modern matched replication remains testable; it would not invalidate the valid formal theorem.
positive_evidence: The dissertation proves exact complexity classifications for its formal decision problems and explicitly scopes itself to lower-bound proofs rather than benchmark studies.
The 2010 follow-up explains the EXPTIME/polynomial split through shared closures versus object representations and derives a polynomial-time context-sensitive hierarchy for functional programs.

The follow-up reports empirical comparisons where m-CFA appears as precise as k-CFA at a fraction of the cost on the tested cases, directly showing theoretical worst-case hardness can coexist with tractable evaluated inputs/variants.
counterevidence: The dissertation's EXPTIME-completeness theorem remains a strong worst-case lower bound for the formal kCFA decision problem it defines; favorable benchmarks cannot erase it.

The follow-up's favorable m-CFA results are conditioned on its benchmark set, definitions, implementation, and precision measures; they do not guarantee the same tradeoff on modern languages or analyses.
This audit reads one dissertation and one closely connected PLDI follow-up; it does not provide a comprehensive survey of CFA complexity or performance.

sources.sections: Abstract and Preface; Chapters 3 and 5; Section 5.6; Chapter 7
Introduction and Sections 2–6: OO/functional representation distinction, polynomial m-CFA construction, empirical precision/cost comparison

falsifiable_test: Reimplement and pin the formal definitions of functional kCFA, OO kCFA, and m-CFA, and compare them on matched functional/OO encodings of common higher-order benchmarks plus generated worst-case stressors. Report precision against a common soundness oracle, wall time, peak memory, and scaling over input size/context depth, with separate results by closure representation. The lead weakens if practical performance is insensitive to the identified representation/context choices or m-CFA fails to match the reported precision-cost tradeoff; it strengthens if measured cost and precision change systematically. No analyses were rerun in this batch.
limitations: The sampled source is a 2009 formal dissertation selected through its 2013 arXiv submission date; the follow-up appeared at PLDI 2010 and is not an independent replication. No benchmark suite was executed here, and no practical runtime claim is inferred from asymptotic completeness alone.
